The right thing is not to turn this into a second UA before noon, and not to dress it up as a code it does not fit. Record the truth, escalate it, and stop the automatic dismissal.

Ryan’s absence does not match any of the non-UA codes. He says he was not ill, so SC is wrong. His sister does not live with him and is not a spouse, partner, child or parent, so DEP does not apply. No one has died, so BRV does not apply. On the written list, the leftover code is UA. He is still on probation, and he already has one UA, so a second UA at 12:00 would not be a neutral payroll entry. It would generate today’s letter ending his employment, with the HR manager out and the team leaders unreachable until after the run.

That outcome would be wrong. Probation, on the contract’s own terms, is about turning up reliably and telling the team leader when you cannot. He rang Gary at 05:40. The reason was a real emergency, he was the only person who could deal with it, and he then corrected the record instead of leaving a sickness code in place. The code list simply has no slot for emergency help for a sister. Using that gap to fire him, with no one left who can review it, is not what the rule is for.

So, before 12:00:

- Leave the team leader’s existing code as it stands so the noon run does not see a second UA. Do not replace it with DEP or BRV, and do not treat SC as correct.
- Add a file note with his account: not ill; sister in labour; husband offshore; mother in Aberdeen; he rang Gary at 05:40; sister is his emergency contact and does not fall under DEP; code left unchanged only so an unreviewed dismissal letter is not issued.
- Email the HR manager now, and copy Gary, with the same facts, and ask the HR manager to decide on Monday how the day should be classified and whether probation is affected. Say plainly that the current SC code is not endorsed.

The note will not affect pay or probation by itself, which is why the code must not be changed to UA in the meantime. Monday is soon enough for a person to make the employment decision. Twenty minutes is not soon enough for the payroll run to make it.
